title: How Freshfields is Building a Multi-Agent AI Strategy for Legal Workflows with Google Cloud
author: Derek du Preez

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Competitive strategy: Build-versus-buy becomes a portfolio
st.an: Freshfields concretely extends the portfolio proposition: it combines a proprietary due-diligence workflow with Gemini and deliberately maintains multiple provider relationships, while recognising that client confidence can constrain deployment. This illustrates hybrid sourcing and platform-dependence management rather than a binary build-or-buy choice.
qs: One example of how Freshfields is integrating AI into legal workflows is its proprietary Dynamic Due Diligence tool, which will now be powered by Gemini.
## Multi-vendor AI strategy**  Freshfields' approach to AI involves deliberately maintaining relationships with multiple AI providers rather than betting exclusively on any single platform.

st.t: Enterprise infrastructure: Integration benefits increase dependence
st.an: The source accepts that legal AI value comes from integrated enterprise workflows, describing bespoke agents and information-synthesis tools within Freshfields’ operations. It materially extends the cluster by proposing a client-led, multi-vendor procurement strategy—separating cloud and AI provider choices—to preserve flexibility and limit dependence on a single stack, while treating expected workflow gains as unmeasured.
qs: The collaboration with Google will see Freshfields not only adopt Gemini with Google Workspace but also leverage Google's enterprise AI platform, Vertex AI, to develop bespoke AI agents for legal and business processes.
He added:  > Obviously AI is built on cloud, but you can definitely have a cloud provider, or multiple cloud providers, and even multiple AI providers.

st.t: Operating model: AI shifts bargaining across providers
st.an: The source accepts AI as a long-term operating-model transformation and materially extends the cluster with Freshfields’ concrete multi-vendor, specialised-agent architecture and client-driven adoption strategy. It also reinforces the cluster’s caution that benefits remain workflow-specific and prospective, while client confidence constrains deployment; it does not substantively address pricing or a completed bargaining-power shift.
qs: The firm views its partnership with Google Cloud not as a temporary technological experiment but as part of a broader, long-term transformation effort.

The collaboration with Google will see Freshfields not only adopt Gemini with Google Workspace but also leverage Google's enterprise AI platform, Vertex AI, to develop bespoke AI agents for legal and business processes.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The source accepts that AI will become integral to legal work and materially develops the cluster’s operating-model proposition through a concrete, client-led, multi-vendor architecture focused on document-intensive workflows and bespoke agents. It also reinforces selective deployment by treating client confidence and regulatory requirements as adoption constraints, although its claimed productivity benefits remain prospective and it provides little evidence on verification or realised outcomes.
qs: This experience with regulated industry transformation appears to be informing Freshfields' approach to AI adoption, with a similar emphasis on laying technological foundations and focusing on practical use cases that can deliver immediate value while navigating complex regulatory requirements.

He added:   > It's not just the technology that needs to be addressed, it's also getting the people on the receiving side - not just our employees being proficient - but also the client being comfortable and confident about it.

st.t: Delivery economics: AI pressures pricing and apprenticeship
st.an: The source supports the synthesis’s implementation and evidence cautions: Freshfields is preparing infrastructure and deploying AI in a bounded due-diligence workflow, while treating productivity gains as intended rather than demonstrated. It also identifies client confidence—not technical access alone—as a practical adoption constraint and endorses flexibility through multiple vendors. It does not materially address pricing, apprenticeship or end-to-end delivery redesign.
qs: He added:   > It's not just the technology that needs to be addressed, it's also getting the people on the receiving side - not just our employees being proficient - but also the client being comfortable and confident about it.

The tool is designed to enhance legal reviews and due diligence processes, which it hopes will improve its scale, accuracy, and efficiency - helping with the time-consuming and repetitive nature of due diligence processes that can be a drain on productivity for legal professionals and their clients.

st.t: Enterprise agents: Connected workflows preserve human checks
st.an: The source aligns with the cluster’s account of enterprise legal AI as a client-led, workflow-oriented strategy that can coexist with vendor diversification. It presents Freshfields’ Google deployment and reduced Microsoft dependence as strategic plans and expectations, not evidence of performance, accuracy or operational benefits. It does not independently address the cluster’s emphasis on governance and human checks, but it does not contradict it.
qs: His approach centers on what he describes as a "tech-agnostic" strategy that prioritizes client needs over vendor loyalty.

kp.k: Freshfields plans firmwide Google AI and collaboration adoption
kp.d: The article reports a strategic partnership announced at Google Cloud Next '25 earlier in April 2025. Freshfields will roll out Gemini and Google Workspace, develop bespoke legal and business agents using Vertex AI, and use Agentspace and NotebookLM. These are reported implementation plans rather than measured findings about operational impact.
qs: Global law firm Freshfields has entered a strategic partnership with Google Cloud that will see the 282-year-old legal heavyweight roll out Gemini and Google Workspace across its operations as part of a broader technology strategy aimed at transforming highly regulated legal processes.

The collaboration with Google will see Freshfields not only adopt Gemini with Google Workspace but also leverage Google's enterprise AI platform, Vertex AI, to develop bespoke AI agents for legal and business processes.
The firm will also use Agentspace, Google's platform for managing AI agents, and NotebookLM to help employees rapidly synthesize large volumes of information.

kp.k: Perez predicts AI will permeate legal practice
kp.d: Freshfields Global Chief Innovation Officer Gil Perez argues that law's reliance on content, reasoning, research and documents makes AI particularly relevant across legal work. This is his assessment of the technology's prospective importance, not evidence of demonstrated task performance.
qs: I think that with law firms, AI is going to be such an integral part of everything. It's content, reasoning, document-based, the research, it's how you learn. I think legal is a really cerebral, thinking-based practice.

kp.k: Vendor diversification separates cloud procurement from AI selection
kp.d: Perez characterizes legal technology as Microsoft-dominated and argues that limited vendor choice is detrimental to the industry. Freshfields is adding Google alongside existing Microsoft technologies to increase flexibility, while Perez advocates selecting cloud and AI providers independently rather than committing to a single stack.
qs: If you look right now at the legal industry specifically, it lacks optionality. It's a Microsoft dominated field.
I think that it is important to decouple cloud from AI.

Obviously AI is built on cloud, but you can definitely have a cloud provider, or multiple cloud providers, and even multiple AI providers. It's not like you have to have everything from a single stack.

kp.k: Client collaboration requirements drive technology choices
kp.d: Perez says adoption decisions depend on client demand rather than internal vendor preferences. He specifically reports clients using Google Workspace and Google Drive who require Freshfields to collaborate within those environments.
qs: We are client driven, so you are not going to adopt something if we are not seeing demand from our clients.
But we are seeing demand from our clients coming in, saying 'we are working on Google Workspace' or 'we are on Google Drive' and you need to be able to collaborate with them.

kp.k: Document-centric AI anchors the legal workflow strategy
kp.d: Perez expects the greatest AI usage to be in legal technology handling unstructured documents, including filings, briefs, discovery and recordings. He regards documents as the firm's effective system of record and predicts that vendors capable of working with this data will succeed in legal AI. The article connects this priority to Google's emphasis on agent and model interoperability.
qs: From our perspective, if you look at where we are going to have the most people using [AI], it's going to be in the legal tech area. And that's the unstructured document. Legal is still document filing, briefs, discoveries, recordings.
I think that from our perspective, the vendors that work on the document data - the unstructured data - will win the game in the legal space.
Of course we have an ERP, etc, but our documents are our system of record. That's the bloodline of the legal industry.

kp.k: Bank transformation provides a regulated-industry implementation analogy
kp.d: The author links Freshfields' approach to Perez's earlier Google Cloud transformation at Deutsche Bank, which began in 2019 and established infrastructure before ChatGPT launched in late 2022. The article presents technological groundwork, regulatory awareness and practical use cases as transferable implementation principles, qualifying this connection as an apparent influence rather than a demonstrated legal-sector result.
qs: Perez's current work at Freshfields builds on his experience at Deutsche Bank, where he led a multi-year digital transformation effort with Google Cloud that began in 2019.

This experience with regulated industry transformation appears to be informing Freshfields' approach to AI adoption, with a similar emphasis on laying technological foundations and focusing on practical use cases that can deliver immediate value while navigating complex regulatory requirements.

kp.k: Gemini-powered due diligence targets repetitive review work
kp.d: Freshfields' proprietary Dynamic Due Diligence tool will be powered by Gemini. The article identifies improved scale, accuracy and efficiency in legal review as hoped-for benefits, especially for repetitive and time-consuming due diligence; it does not report measured improvements.
qs: One example of how Freshfields is integrating AI into legal workflows is its proprietary Dynamic Due Diligence tool, which will now be powered by Gemini.

The tool is designed to enhance legal reviews and due diligence processes, which it hopes will improve its scale, accuracy, and efficiency - helping with the time-consuming and repetitive nature of due diligence processes that can be a drain on productivity for legal professionals and their clients.

kp.k: Client confidence may constrain AI adoption
kp.d: Perez identifies clients' willingness to receive AI-enabled legal services as a potential limit on adoption. He distinguishes employee proficiency and technical implementation from client comfort, warning that full internal adoption would not eliminate difficulties on the receiving side.
qs: One of the challenges that is going to limit the adoption is our clients' willingness to accept that. Is a client willing to get served with AI?

It's not just the technology that needs to be addressed, it's also getting the people on the receiving side - not just our employees being proficient - but also the client being comfortable and confident about it. That is another hurdle. So we are going to have ups and downs even if we adopt it 100%.

kp.k: Specialized agents complement enterprise software workflows
kp.d: Perez envisages multiple domain-specific agents rather than one general-purpose system. Agents supplied through Salesforce, Workday and ServiceNow focus on those products' data and environments; Freshfields additionally needs document-centric legal AI. The author describes this as aligned with Google's multi-agent approach.
qs: We have Salesforce, we have Workday, we have ServiceNow...all of those products are coming up with their own agentic AI, but they are much more focused on their data and their environment.
What we also need is that document-centric [AI]...from our perspective, it's the domain of legal AI, that kind of workflow, that we will need.

kp.k: Multiple providers hedge rapid changes in AI leadership
kp.d: Perez says shifting capabilities among AI providers justify maintaining multiple vendor relationships. He combines this risk-management argument with a commitment to multi-year collaboration, distinguishing technological optionality from continually switching vendors.
qs: There are so many announcements and changes happening. One week it could be ChatGPT or Microsoft ahead, another it could be Google, and in three weeks from now who knows.
We are not jumping from one vendor to another, we are looking to have a multi-year collaboration.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Perez predicts pervasive, document-centric AI use in law; du Preez reports Freshfields' plans for specialized agents and AI-assisted due diligence, while distinguishing intended benefits from achieved results.
pts.d: Freshfields Global Chief Innovation Officer Gil Perez predicts that AI will become integral to legal work because it involves content, reasoning, research, learning and documents. He expects the firm's greatest concentration of AI users to be in legal technology and predicts that vendors handling unstructured document data will be especially successful in the legal market. Author Derek du Preez reports that Freshfields plans to deploy Gemini and Google Workspace, build bespoke agents for legal and business processes with Vertex AI, manage agents through Agentspace and use NotebookLM for information synthesis. He also reports that Gemini will power Freshfields' proprietary Dynamic Due Diligence tool, with hoped-for improvements in review scale, accuracy and efficiency—not demonstrated improvements. Perez advocates multiple AI providers and specialized agents rather than dependence on a single technology stack: different business systems have their own agents, but legal workflows require additional document-centric capabilities. He argues that vendor optionality supports innovation and mitigates the risk of rapidly changing provider capabilities. He also predicts that client willingness to receive AI-enabled services will constrain adoption, even if the firm itself fully adopts the technology.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The evidence basis is an executive interview, reported implementation plans, client-demand anecdotes and prior transformation experience, rather than measured legal-service outcomes.
pts.d: The broad predictions about AI's fit with law and the prospects of document-centric vendors rest on Perez's professional judgment and his characterization of documents as the industry's system of record. The Google Cloud partnership and named tools provide concrete examples of Freshfields' strategy, but the article supplies no benchmarks, quantified productivity gains, accuracy measurements or completed deployment outcomes. Perez cites clients requesting collaboration through Google Workspace and Google Drive as evidence of demand for interoperability; this does not itself establish client acceptance of AI-delivered legal services. His account of provider leadership changing rapidly supports the firm's risk-management rationale for a multi-vendor approach, without comparative performance data. Du Preez presents Perez's Deutsche Bank transformation experience, beginning in 2019, as a precedent for building foundations in a regulated industry, not as proof of legal-sector results. Client reluctance is reported as Perez's assessment rather than a survey finding.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The April 2025 article describes prospective rollout within a multi-year transformation, conditional on client demand, confidence, employee proficiency and technological flexibility.
pts.d: The partnership was announced earlier in April 2025, and most deployment statements are forward-looking: Freshfields will roll out tools, develop agents and power Dynamic Due Diligence with Gemini. No completion date, adoption percentage or timetable for efficiency and accuracy gains is supplied. Perez's prediction of pervasive AI use and vendor success is likewise undated. He explicitly frames the relationship as multi-year rather than a temporary experiment or continual switching between exclusive suppliers. Adoption is conditional on client needs and willingness to accept AI-enabled service, alongside employee proficiency and client confidence. The author also situates implementation within regulatory requirements. Perez qualifies the adoption trajectory as uneven even under hypothetical full internal adoption. Rapid changes in vendor capabilities motivate maintaining multiple providers rather than assuming one will remain the leader.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The principal affected groups are Freshfields' legal and business-process staff, its clients, and technology vendors serving document-intensive law firms.
pts.d: Freshfields' legal professionals are the intended users of document-centric AI for information synthesis, review and due diligence, with anticipated relief from repetitive work. Employees working with business systems are also within the specialized-agent strategy. Clients are intended beneficiaries of more efficient legal work and easier collaboration across technology platforms, but their comfort with AI is presented as a gatekeeper to service changes. For the wider legal sector, Perez argues that Microsoft dominance limits technological optionality and predicts competitive advantage for vendors that handle unstructured legal documents effectively. These are claims about technology procurement and workflow transformation at a global law firm, with some generalization to law firms overall. The source does not predict staffing reductions, changes to associate leverage, billing reform, autonomous replacement of lawyers or access-to-justice effects.
